215removed-- ## The `simp` Tactic
216removed
217removed-- The lemmas we've been using for rewriting are the same ones
218removed-- we'll give to `simp` for it to automatically solve goals
219removed-- involving those theorems.
220removed
221removed-- We tag theorems with `@[simp]` to add them to the set of
222removed-- rules `simp` considers when simplifying a term.
223removed
224removednamespace simp_lemmas_example
225removed
226removed/- `add_zero` and `add_succ` are the `simp` lemmas for `+`. -/
227removed@[simp]
228removedtheorem add_zero (n : Nat) : n + 0 = n := by rfl
229removed
230removed@[simp]
231removedtheorem add_succ (n m : Nat) : n + (m + 1) = (n + m) + 1:= by rfl
232removed
233removed-- Instead of manually rewriting by the characterizing lemmas
234removed-- in the example below, `simp` does it automatically.
235removed
236removedtheorem add_succ_nested (n m : Nat) :
237removed n + (m + 1 + 1) = (n + m + 1) + 1 := by
238removed simp
239removed
240removed-- `simp only` uses only the provided theorems:
241removed
242removedtheorem add_succ_nested_2 (n m : Nat) :
243removed n + (m + 1 + 1) = (n + m + 1) + 1 := by
244removed simp only [add_succ, add_zero]
245removed
246removed-- If you want to know what `simp` is doing, you can run
247removed-- `simp?`.
248removed
249removedtheorem add_succ_nested_3 (n m : Nat) :
250removed n + (m + 1 + 1) = (n + m + 1) + 1 := by
251removed simp?
252removed
253removedend simp_lemmas_example

271removed intro h₁ h₂

290removed intro hPerm hIn

293removed-- ### Idiomatic `simp` Usage
294removed
295removed-- Don't use `simp` without `only` unless you're closing a goal
296removed-- or following with a flexible tactic, like in this example
297removed-- below:
298removed
299removedexample α x (l₁ l₂ l₃ : List α) :
300removed x ∈ l₁ ++ l₂ →
301removed x ∈ l₂ ++ l₃ ->
302removed x ∈ l₁ ++ l₃ ∨ x ∈ l₂ := by
303removed intro h₁ h₂
304removed
305removed simp at h₁; simp at h₂; simp
306removed cases h₁ with
307removed | inl h => left; left; exact h
308removed | inr h => right; exact h
309removed
310removed-- This usage of `simp` is brittle and can break due to
311removed-- upstream changes.
312removed
313removed-- We can fix the style of this proof by changing the `simp`s
314removed-- to specify which theorems they are using to simplify:
315removed
316removedexample α x (l₁ l₂ l₃ : List α) :
317removed x ∈ l₁ ++ l₂ →
318removed x ∈ l₂ ++ l₃ ->
319removed x ∈ l₁ ++ l₃ ∨ x ∈ l₂ := by
320removed intro h₁ h₂
321removed
322removed -- the * here targets all hypotheses and the goal
323removed simp only [List.mem_append] at *
324removed cases h₁ with
325removed | inl h => left; left; exact h
326removed | inr h => right; exact h
327removed

338removed-- ## The `trivial` tactic
339removed
340removed-- A final automated tactic to have in your toolkit is
341removed-- `trivial`, which tries a number of different simple tactics
342removed-- (such as `rfl` or `contradiction`) to try to close the
343removed-- current goal. Some examples:
344removed
345removedexample : 1 = 1 := by trivial
346removedexample : (1, 2).fst = 1 := by trivial
347removedexample (A B : Prop) : ¬ A -> A -> B := by intro h₁ h₂; trivial
348removed
349removed-- ## Case Study: Regular Expressions
350removed
351removed-- ### Definitions
352removed
353removedinductive RegExp (α : Type) : Type where
354removed | EmptySet
355removed | EmptyStr
356removed | Char (c : α)
357removed | App (r1 r2 : RegExp α)
358removed | Union (r1 r2 : RegExp α)
359removed | Star (r : RegExp α)
360removedderiving BEq, DecidableEq, Repr
361removed
362removedattribute [pp_nodot] RegExp.Char RegExp.App RegExp.Union RegExp.Star
363removed
364removed-- Note that this definition is *polymorphic*: Regular
365removed-- expressions in `RegExp α` describe strings with characters
366removed-- drawn from `α` -- which in this exercise we represent as
367removed-- *lists* with elements from `α`.
368removed
369removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @@dsainati1):
370removed-- CH: Do you mean here that this is different because the
371removed-- inductive type doesn't specify α is finite? In Lean the
372removed-- convention is for inductives not to carry Prop-valued
373removed-- typeclasss assumptions, enforcing this only at the
374removed-- theorems that use them. So this could give off a
375removed-- slightly wrong impression. DHS: @bcpierce00 What was the
376removed-- purpose of this aside in the original Rocq text? Does it
377removed-- make sense to keep here?
378removed
379removed-- We connect regular expressions and strings by defining when
380removed-- a regular expression *matches* some string.
381removed
382removed-- Informally this looks as follows:
383removed
384removed-- - The regular expression `EmptySet` does not match any string.
385removed
386removed-- - `EmptyString` matches the empty string `[]`.
387removed
388removed-- - `Char x` matches the one-character string `x`.
389removed
390removed-- - If `re₁` matches `s₁`, and `re₂` matches `s₂`, then
391removed-- `App re₁ re₂` matches `s₁ ++ s₂`.
392removed
393removed-- - If at least one of `re₁` and `re₂` matches `s`, then
394removed-- `Union re₁ re₂` matches `s`.
395removed
396removed-- - Finally, if we can write some string `s` as the
397removed-- concatenation of a sequence of strings
398removed-- `s = s_1 ++ ... ++ s_k`, and the expression `re` matches
399removed-- each one of the strings `s_i`, then `Star re` matches `s`.
400removed
401removed-- In particular, the sequence of strings may be empty, so
402removed-- `Star re` always matches the empty string `[]` no matter
403removed-- what `re` is.
404removed
405removed-- We can easily translate this intuition into a set of rules,
406removed-- where we write `s =~ re` to say that `re` matches `s`:
407removed
408removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
409removed-- Check typesetting here (rules should be centered, I
410removed-- think):
411removed
412removed-- ─────────────── (mEmpty)
413removed-- [] =~ EmptyStr
414removed
415removed-- ─────────────── (mChar)
416removed-- [x] =~ (Char x)
417removed
418removed-- s₁ =~ re₁ s₂ =~ re₂
419removed-- ─────────────────────────── (mApp)
420removed-- (s₁ ++ s₂) =~ (App re₁ re₂)
421removed
422removed-- s₁ =~ re₁
423removed-- ───────────────────── (mUnionL)
424removed-- s₁ =~ (Union re₁ re₂)
425removed
426removed-- s₂ =~ re₂
427removed-- ───────────────────── (mUnionR)
428removed-- s₂ =~ (Union re₁ re₂)
429removed
430removed-- ──────────────── (mStar0)
431removed-- [] =~ (Star re)
432removed
433removed-- s₁ =~ re s₂ =~ (Star re)
434removed-- ──────────────────────────── (mStarApp)
435removed-- (s₁ ++ s₂) =~ (Star re)
436removed
437removed-- This directly corresponds to the following `inductive`
438removed-- definition:
439removed
440removednamespace RegExp
441removedinductive ExpMatch {α : Type} : List α → RegExp α → Prop where
442removed | mEmpty : ExpMatch [] EmptyStr
443removed | mChar (c : α) : ExpMatch [c] (Char c)
444removed | mApp (s₁ : List α) (re₁ : RegExp α) (s₂ : List α) (re₂ : RegExp α)
445removed (h₁ : ExpMatch s₁ re₁) (h₂ : ExpMatch s₂ re₂)
446removed : ExpMatch (s₁ ++ s₂) (App re₁ re₂)
447removed | mUnionL (s₁ : List α) (re₁ : RegExp α) (re₂ : RegExp α)
448removed (h₁ : ExpMatch s₁ re₁) : ExpMatch s₁ (Union re₁ re₂)
449removed | mUnionR (s₂ : List α) (re₁ : RegExp α) (re₂ : RegExp α)
450removed (h₂ : ExpMatch s₂ re₂) : ExpMatch s₂ (Union re₁ re₂)
451removed | mStar0 (re : RegExp α) : ExpMatch [] (Star re)
452removed | mStarApp (s₁ s₂ : List α) (re : RegExp α)
453removed (h₁ : ExpMatch s₁ re) (h₂ : ExpMatch s₂ (Star re))
454removed : ExpMatch (s₁ ++ s₂) (Star re)
455removed
456removedinfix:40 " =~ " => ExpMatch
457removed
458removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @@dsainati1):
459removed-- replace with quiz directive
460removed
461removedtheorem quiz α (s: List α) : ¬(s =~ EmptySet) := by
462removed intro contra; inversion contra
463removed
464removed-- ### Examples
465removed
466removedexample : [1] =~ Char 1 := by
467removed apply ExpMatch.mChar
468removed
469removedexample : [1, 2] =~ App (Char 1) (Char 2):= by
470removed apply ExpMatch.mApp [1] <;> constructor
471removed
472removedexample : ¬([1, 2] =~ Char 1) := by
473removed intro contra; inversion contra
474removed
475removed-- We can define helper functions for writing down regular
476removed-- expressions. The `reg_exp_of_list` function constructs a
477removed-- regular expression that matches exactly the string that it
478removed-- receives as an argument:
479removed
480removeddef reg_exp_of_list {α} (l : List α) :=
481removed match l with
482removed | [] => EmptyStr
483removed | x :: l' => App (Char x) (reg_exp_of_list l')
484removed
485removedexample : [1, 2, 3] =~ reg_exp_of_list [1, 2, 3] := by
486removed apply ExpMatch.mApp [1]; constructor
487removed apply ExpMatch.mApp [2]; constructor
488removed apply ExpMatch.mApp [3]; constructor
489removed constructor
490removed
491removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): regexp_match_of_list ⭐
492removed
493removed-- As a quick exercise, prove that every list matches
494removed-- `reg_exp_of_list` of itself:
495removed
496removedtheorem regexp_match_of_list α (l : List α) : l =~ reg_exp_of_list l := by
497removed sorry
498removed
499removed-- Something more interesting:
500removed
501removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @@dsainati1):
502removed-- How to make this a WORKINCLASS in verso?
503removed
504removedtheorem MStar1 α s (re : RegExp α) :
505removed s =~ re →
506removed s =~ Star re := by
507removed intro h
508removed rw [← List.append_nil s]
509removed constructor
510removed . assumption
511removed . constructor
512removed
513removed-- The following lemmas show that the intuition about matching
514removed-- given at the beginning of the section can be obtained from
515removed-- the formal inductive definition.
516removed
517removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): EmptySet_is_empty ⭐
518removed
519removedtheorem EmptySet_is_empty α (s : List α) : ¬(s =~ EmptySet) := by
520removed sorry
521removed
522removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): MUnion' ⭐
523removed
524removedtheorem MUnion' α (s : List α) (re₁ re₂ : RegExp α) :
525removed s =~ re₁ ∨ s =~ re₂ →
526removed s =~ Union re₁ re₂ := by
527removed sorry
528removed
529removed-- The next lemma is stated in terms of the `fold` function on
530removed-- Lists: If `ss : List (List α)` represents a sequence of
531removed-- strings `s₁, ..., sn`, then `List.foldr (· ++ ·) ss []` is
532removed-- the result of concatenating them all together.
533removed
534removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): MUnion' ⭐⭐
535removed
536removedtheorem MStar' α (ss : List (List α)) (re : RegExp α)
537removed (h : ∀ s, s ∈ ss → s =~ re) :
538removed ss.foldr (· ++ ·) [] =~ RegExp.Star re := by
539removed -- ADMITTED
540removed induction ss with
541removed | nil => constructor
542removed | cons s ss' ih =>
543removed simp
544removed constructor
545removed · apply h; simp
546removed · apply ih; intro s' hs'
547removed apply h; right; assumption
548removed
549removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): EmptyStr_not_needed ⭐
550removed
551removed-- It turns out that the `EmptyStr` constructor is actually not
552removed-- needed, since the regular expression matching the empty
553removed-- string can also be defined from `Star` and `EmptySet`:
554removed
555removeddef EmptyStr' {α:Type} := @Star α (EmptySet)
556removed
557removed-- State and prove that this `EmptyStr'` definition matches
558removed-- exactly the same strings as the `EmptyStr` constructor.
559removed
560removed-- Naturally, proofs about `ExpMatch` often require induction
561removed-- (on evidence!).
562removed
563removed-- For example, suppose we want to prove the following
564removed-- intuitive fact: If a string `s` is matched by a regular
565removed-- expression `re`, then all elements of `s` must occur as
566removed-- character literals somewhere in `re`.
567removed
568removed-- To state this as a theorem, we first define a function
569removed-- `re_chars` that lists all characters that occur in a regular
570removed-- expression:
571removed
572removeddef reChars {α : Type} (re : RegExp α) : List α :=
573removed match re with
574removed | EmptySet => []
575removed | EmptyStr => []
576removed | Char x => [x]
577removed | App re₁ re₂ => reChars re₁ ++ reChars re₂
578removed | Union re₁ re₂ => reChars re₁ ++ reChars re₂
579removed | Star re => reChars re
580removed
581removed-- Now, the main theorem:
582removed
583removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @@dsainati1):
584removed-- This should be a workinclass
585removed
586removedtheorem in_re_match {α : Type} {s : List α} {re : RegExp α} {x : α}
587removed (hmatch : s =~ re) (hin : x ∈ s) : x ∈ reChars re := by
588removed induction hmatch with
589removed | mEmpty => simp at hin
590removed | mChar c => simp [reChars]; simp at hin; exact hin
591removed | mApp _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
592removed
593removed /- Something interesting happens in the `mApp` case. We obtain
594removed _two_ induction hypotheses: One that applies when `x` occurs in
595removed `s₁` (which is matched by `re₁`), and a second one that applies when `x`
596removed occurs in `s₂` (matched by `re₂`). -/
597removed simp [reChars] at *
598removed rcases hin with hin₁ | hin₂
599removed · left; exact ih₁ hin₁
600removed · right; exact ih₂ hin₂
601removed | mUnionL _ _ _ _ ih =>
602removed simp [reChars]; left; exact ih hin
603removed | mUnionR _ _ _ h₂ ih =>
604removed simp [reChars]; right; exact ih hin
605removed | mStar0 => simp at hin
606removed | mStarApp _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
607removed
608removed /- Here again we get two induction hypotheses, and they illustrate
609removed why we need induction on evidence for `ExpMatch`, rather than
610removed induction on the regular expression `re`: The latter would only
611removed provide an induction hypothesis for strings that match `re`, which
612removed would not allow us to reason about the case `In x ∈ s₂`. -/
613removed simp at hin
614removed rcases hin with hin₁ | hin₂
615removed · exact ih₁ hin₁
616removed · exact ih₂ hin₂
617removed
618removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): reNotEmpty ⭐
619removed
620removed-- Write a recursive function `reNotEmpty` that tests whether a
621removed-- regular expression matches some string. Prove that your
622removed-- function is correct.
623removed
624removed-- ### The `generalize` Tactic
625removed
626removed-- One potentially confusing feature of the `induction` tactic
627removed-- is that it won't let you perform an induction over a term
628removed-- that isn't sufficiently general. Here's an example:
629removed
630removed/--
631removederror: Invalid target: Index in target's type is not a variable (consider using the `cases` tactic instead)
632removed Star re
633removed-/
634removed#guard_msgs in
635removedexample α (s₁ s₂ : List α) (re : RegExp α) :
636removed s₁ =~ Star re →
637removed s₂ =~ Star re →
638removed s₁ ++ s₂ =~ Star re := by
639removed intro h₁
640removed
641removed /- Now, just doing an `inversion` on `h₁` won't get us very far in
642removed the recursive cases. (Try it!). So we need induction (on
643removed evidence). We might try this, but Lean won't let us: -/
644removed induction h₁
645removed
646removed-- The problem here is that `induction` over a Prop hypothesis
647removed-- only works properly with hypotheses that are "fully
648removed-- general," i.e., ones in which all the arguments are just
649removed-- variables, as opposed to more specific expressions like
650removed-- `Star re`.
651removed
652removed-- A possible, but awkward, way to solve this problem is
653removed-- "manually generalizing" over the problematic expressions by
654removed-- adding explicit equality hypotheses to the lemma:
655removed
656removedexample α (s₁ s₂ : List α) (re re' : RegExp α) :
657removed re' = Star re →
658removed s₁ =~ re' →
659removed s₂ =~ Star re →
660removed s₁ ++ s₂ =~ Star re := by
661removed
662removed intro h₁ h₂ h₃
663removed/- We can now proceed by performing induction over evidence
664removed directly, because the argument to the first hypothesis is
665removed sufficiently general, which means that we can discharge most cases
666removed by inverting the `re' = Star re` equality in the context. *)
667removed This works, but it makes the statement of the lemma a bit ugly.
668removed Fortunately, there is a better way... -/
669removed sorry
670removed
671removed-- The tactic `generalize h : e = x` causes Lean to (1) replace
672removed-- all occurrences of the expression `e` by the variable `x`,
673removed-- and (2) add an equation `h : x = e` to the context. Here's
674removed-- how we can use it to show the above result:
675removed
676removedtheorem star_app α (s₁ s₂ : List α) (re : RegExp α) :
677removed s₁ =~ Star re →
678removed s₂ =~ Star re →
679removed s₁ ++ s₂ =~ Star re := by
680removed
681removed intro h₁
682removed generalize heq : Star re = re' at h₁
683removed -- We now have `heq : Star re = re'`
684removed -- `heq` is contradictory in most cases, allowing us to conclude immediately via `contradiction`
685removed induction h₁ <;> try contradiction
686removed -- The interesting cases are those that correspond to `Star`
687removed case mStar0 _ => intro h₂; simp only [List.nil_append]; exact h₂
688removed case mStarApp _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₂ =>
689removed injections heq; subst heq
690removed intro h₂; simp only [List.append_assoc]
691removed apply ExpMatch.mStarApp
692removed . assumption
693removed . apply ih₂ <;> trivial
694removed /- Note that the induction hypothesis `ih₂` on the `mStarApp` case
695removed mentions an additional premise [Star re'' = Star re], which
696removed results from the equality generated by `generalize`. -/
697removed
698removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): exp_match_ex2 ⭐
699removed
700removed-- The `MStar''` lemma below (combined with its converse, the
701removed-- `MStar'` exercise above), shows that our definition of
702removed-- `ExpMatch` for `Star` is equivalent to the informal one
703removed-- given previously.
704removed
705removedtheorem MStar'' α (s : List α) (re : RegExp α) :
706removed s =~ Star re →
707removed exists ss : List (List α),
708removed s = List.foldr (· ++ ·) [] ss
709removed ∧ ∀ s', s' ∈ ss → s' =~ re := by
710removed sorry
711removed
712removed-- ### The "Weak" Pumping Lemma
713removed
714removed-- One of the first really interesting theorems in the theory
715removed-- of regular expressions is the so-called *pumping lemma*,
716removed-- which states, informally, that any sufficiently long string
717removed-- `s` matching a regular expression `re` can be "pumped" by
718removed-- repeating some middle section of `s` an arbitrary number of
719removed-- times to produce a new string also matching `re`. For the
720removed-- sake of simplicity, this exercise considers a slightly
721removed-- weaker theorem than is usually stated in courses on automata
722removed-- theory -- hence the name `weak_pumping`. The stronger one
723removed-- can be found below.
724removed
725removed-- To get started, we need to define "sufficiently long." Since
726removed-- we are working in a constructive logic, we actually need to
727removed-- be able to *calculate*, for each regular expression `re`, a
728removed-- minimum length for strings `s` to guarantee "pumpability."
729removed
730removednamespace Pumping
731removed
732removeddef pumpingConstant {α : Type} (re : RegExp α) : Nat :=
733removed match re with
734removed | RegExp.EmptySet => 1
735removed | RegExp.EmptyStr => 1
736removed | RegExp.Char _ => 2
737removed | RegExp.App re₁ re₂ => pumpingConstant re₁ + pumpingConstant re₂
738removed | RegExp.Union re₁ re₂ => pumpingConstant re₁ + pumpingConstant re₂
739removed | RegExp.Star r => pumpingConstant r
740removed
741removed-- You may find these lemmas about the pumping constant useful
742removed-- when proving the pumping lemma below.
743removed
744removedtheorem pumping_constant_ge_1 {α : Type} (re : RegExp α) :
745removed pumpingConstant re ≥ 1 := by
746removed induction re with
747removed | EmptySet => simp [pumpingConstant]
748removed | EmptyStr => simp [pumpingConstant]
749removed | Char _ => simp [pumpingConstant]
750removed | App re₁ _ ih1 _ => simp [pumpingConstant]; lia
751removed | Union re₁ _ ih1 _ => simp [pumpingConstant]; lia
752removed | Star _ ih => simp [pumpingConstant]; exact ih
753removed
754removedtheorem pumping_constant_0_false {α : Type} (re : RegExp α)
755removed (h : pumpingConstant re = 0) : False := by
756removed have := pumping_constant_ge_1 re; lia
757removed
758removed-- Next, it is useful to define an auxiliary function that
759removed-- repeats a string (appends it to itself) some number of
760removed-- times. Note how we define `simp` lemmas for `napp` to go
761removed-- with its definition.
762removed
763removeddef napp {α : Type} (n : Nat) (l : List α) : List α :=
764removed match n with
765removed | 0 => []
766removed | n' + 1 => l ++ napp n' l
767removed
768removed@[simp]
769removedtheorem napp_zero {α : Type} (l : List α) : napp 0 l = [] := by rfl
770removed
771removed@[simp]
772removedtheorem napp_succ {α : Type} (n : Nat) (l : List α) : napp (n + 1) l = l ++ napp n l := by rfl
773removed
774removed-- These auxiliary lemmas might also be useful in your proof of
775removed-- the pumping lemma.
776removed
777removed@[simp]
778removedtheorem napp_plus {α : Type} (n m : Nat) (l : List α) :
779removed napp (n + m) l = napp n l ++ napp m l := by
780removed induction n with
781removed | zero => simp
782removed | succ n ih => rw [Nat.succ_add]; simp [ih]
783removed
784removedtheorem napp_star {α : Type} (m : Nat) (s₁ s₂ : List α) (re : RegExp α)
785removed (hs1 : s₁ =~ re) (hs₂ : s₂ =~ RegExp.Star re) :
786removed napp m s₁ ++ s₂ =~ RegExp.Star re := by
787removed induction m with
788removed | zero => simp only [napp_zero, List.nil_append]; trivial
789removed | succ m ih =>
790removed simp only [napp_succ]
791removed rw [List.append_assoc]
792removed apply ExpMatch.mStarApp <;> trivial
793removed
794removed-- The (weak) pumping lemma itself says that, if `s =~ re` and
795removed-- if the length of `s` is at least the pumping constant of
796removed-- `re`, then `s` can be split into three substrings
797removed-- `s₁ ++ s₂ ++ s₃` in such a way that `s₂` can be repeated any
798removed-- number of times and the result, when combined with `s₁` and
799removed-- `s₃`, will still match `re`. Since `s₂` is also guaranteed
800removed-- not to be the empty string, this gives us a (constructive!)
801removed-- way to generate strings matching `re` that are as long as we
802removed-- like.
803removed
804removed-- This proof is quite long, so to make it more tractable we've
805removed-- broken it up into a number of sub-proofs, which we then
806removed-- assemble to prove the main lemma.
807removed
808removed-- Your job is to complete the proofs of the helper lemmas; the
809removed-- main lemma relies on these. Several of the lemmas about
810removed-- `Nat.ble` that were in an optional exercise earlier in the
811removed-- `IndProp` chapter may be useful here -- in particular,
812removed-- `lt_ge_cases` and `plus_le`
813removed
814removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): weak_pumping_char ⭐⭐
815removed
816removedtheorem weak_pumping_char {α : Type} (x : α) :
817removed pumpingConstant (Char x) ≤ [x].length →
818removed ∃ s₁ s₂ s₃ : List α,
819removed [x] = s₁ ++ s₂ ++ s₃ ∧ s₂ ≠ [ ] ∧
820removed (∀ m : Nat, s₁ ++ napp m s₂ ++ s₃ =~ Char x) := by
821removed sorry
822removed
823removed-- ### Exercise (4 stars): weak_pumping_app ⭐⭐⭐⭐
824removed
825removedtheorem weak_pumping_app {α : Type}
826removed (s₁ s₂ : List α) (re₁ re₂ : RegExp α) :
827removed s₁ =~ re₁ →
828removed s₂ =~ re₂ →
829removed (pumpingConstant re₁ ≤ s₁.length →
830removed ∃ s₂ s₃ s₄ : List α,
831removed s₁ = s₂ ++ s₃ ++ s₄ ∧
832removed s₃ ≠ [ ] ∧
833removed (∀ m : Nat, s₂ ++ napp m s₃ ++ s₄ =~ re₁)) →
834removed (pumpingConstant re₂ ≤ s₂.length →
835removed ∃ s₁ s₃ s₄ : List α,
836removed s₂ = s₁ ++ s₃ ++ s₄ ∧
837removed s₃ ≠ [ ] ∧
838removed (∀ m : Nat, s₁ ++ napp m s₃ ++ s₄ =~ re₂)) →
839removed pumpingConstant (App re₁ re₂) ≤ (s₁ ++ s₂).length →
840removed ∃ s₀ s₃ s₄ : List α,
841removed s₁ ++ s₂ = s₀ ++ s₃ ++ s₄ ∧
842removed s₃ ≠ [ ] ∧
843removed (∀ m : Nat, s₀ ++ napp m s₃ ++ s₄ =~ App re₁ re₂) := by
844removed intro hmatch₁ hMatch2 ih₁ ih₂ hLen
845removed obtain H | H :
846removed pumpingConstant re₁ ≤ s₁.length ∨ pumpingConstant re₂ ≤ s₂.length := by
847removed sorry
848removed . sorry
849removed . sorry
850removed
851removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): weak_pumping_union_l ⭐⭐⭐
852removed
853removedtheorem weak_pumping_union_l {α : Type} (s₁ : List α) (re₁ re₂ : RegExp α) :
854removed s₁ =~ re₁ →
855removed (pumpingConstant re₁ ≤ s₁.length →
856removed ∃ s₂ s₃ s₄ : List α,
857removed s₁ = s₂ ++ s₃ ++ s₄ ∧
858removed s₃ ≠ [ ] ∧
859removed (∀ m : Nat, s₂ ++ napp m s₃ ++ s₄ =~ re₁)) →
860removed pumpingConstant (Union re₁ re₂) ≤ s₁.length →
861removed ∃ s₀ s₂ s₃ : List α,
862removed s₁ = s₀ ++ s₂ ++ s₃ ∧
863removed s₂ ≠ [ ] ∧
864removed (∀ m : Nat, s₀ ++ napp m s₂ ++ s₃ =~ Union re₁ re₂) := by
865removed intro hMatch ih hLen
866removed have h : pumpingConstant re₁ ≤ s₁.length := by
867removed sorry
868removed sorry
869removed
870removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): weak_pumping_union_r ⭐⭐⭐
871removed
872removedtheorem weak_pumping_union_r {α : Type} (s₂ : List α) (re₁ re₂ : RegExp α) :
873removed s₂ =~ re₂ →
874removed (pumpingConstant re₂ ≤ s₂.length →
875removed ∃ s₁ s₃ s₄ : List α,
876removed s₂ = s₁ ++ s₃ ++ s₄ ∧
877removed s₃ ≠ [ ] ∧
878removed (∀ m : Nat, s₁ ++ napp m s₃ ++ s₄ =~ re₂)) →
879removed pumpingConstant (Union re₁ re₂) ≤ s₂.length →
880removed ∃ s₁ s₀ s₃ : List α,
881removed s₂ = s₁ ++ s₀ ++ s₃ ∧
882removed s₀ ≠ [ ] ∧
883removed (∀ m : Nat, s₁ ++ napp m s₀ ++ s₃ =~ Union re₁ re₂) := by
884removed -- symmetric to the previous
885removed intro hMatch ih hLen
886removed have H : pumpingConstant re₂ ≤ s₂.length := by
887removed sorry
888removed sorry
889removed
890removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): weak_pumping_star_zero ⭐⭐
891removed
892removedtheorem weak_pumping_star_zero {α : Type} (re : RegExp α) :
893removed pumpingConstant (Star re) ≤ @List.length α [] →
894removed ∃ s₁ s₂ s₃ : List α,
895removed [ ] = s₁ ++ s₂ ++ s₃ ∧
896removed s₂ ≠ [ ] ∧
897removed (∀ m : Nat, s₁ ++ napp m s₂ ++ s₃ =~ Star re) := by
898removed sorry
899removed
900removed-- ### Exercise (5 stars): weak_pumping_star_app ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
901removed
902removedtheorem weak_pumping_star_app {α : Type} (s₁ s₂ : List α) (re : RegExp α) :
903removed s₁ =~ re →
904removed s₂ =~ .Star re →
905removed (pumpingConstant re ≤ List.length s₁ →
906removed ∃ s₂ s₃ s₄ : List α,
907removed s₁ = s₂ ++ s₃ ++ s₄
908removed ∧ s₃ ≠ [ ] ∧
909removed (∀ m : Nat, s₂ ++ napp m s₃ ++ s₄ =~ re)) →
910removed (pumpingConstant (Star re) ≤ s₂.length →
911removed ∃ s₁ s₃ s₄ : List α,
912removed s₂ = s₁ ++ s₃ ++ s₄ ∧
913removed s₃ ≠ [ ] ∧
914removed (∀ m : Nat, s₁ ++ napp m s₃ ++ s₄ =~ Star re)) →
915removed pumpingConstant (Star re) ≤ (s₁ ++ s₂).length →
916removed ∃ s₀ s₃ s₄ : List α,
917removed s₁ ++ s₂ = s₀ ++ s₃ ++ s₄ ∧
918removed s₃ ≠ [ ] ∧
919removed (∀ m : Nat, s₀ ++ napp m s₃ ++ s₄ =~ .Star re) := by
920removed intro hmatch₁ hmatch₂ ih₁ ih₂ hLen
921removed rw [app_length] at *
922removed obtain Hs1len0 | ⟨s1len, Hs1re1⟩ | Hs1re1 :
923removed (s₁.length = 0
924removed ∨ (s₁.length ≠ 0 ∧ s₁.length < pumpingConstant re)
925removed ∨ pumpingConstant re ≤ s₁.length) := by
926removed cases s₁
927removed . sorry
928removed . case cons h s1' =>
929removed sorry
930removed . sorry
931removed . sorry
932removed . sorry
933removed
934removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): weak_pumping ⭐⭐⭐
935removed
936removedtheorem weak_pumping {α : Type} {re : RegExp α} {s : List α}
937removed (hmatch : s =~ re) (hlen : pumpingConstant re ≤ s.length) :
938removed ∃ s₁ s₂ s₃ : List α,
939removed s = s₁ ++ s₂ ++ s₃ ∧ s₂ ≠ [] ∧
940removed ∀ m, s₁ ++ napp m s₂ ++ s₃ =~ re := by
941removed sorry
942removed
943removed-- ### The (Strong) Pumping Lemma
944removed
945removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @@dsainati1):
946removed-- If this exercise is going to be optional we should still
947removed-- fill in the solution but it's lower priority.
948removed
949removed-- ### Exercise (10 stars): weak_pumping ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
950removed
951removed-- Now here is the usual version of the pumping lemma. In
952removed-- addition to requiring that `s₂ <> []`, it also strengthens
953removed-- the result to include the claim that
954removed-- `length s₁ + length s₂ ≤ pumping_constant re`.
955removed
956removedtheorem pumping {α : Type} {re : RegExp α} {s : List α}
957removed (_hmatch : s =~ re) (_hlen : pumpingConstant re ≤ s.length) :
958removed ∃ s₁ s₂ s₃ : List α,
959removed s = s₁ ++ s₂ ++ s₃ ∧ s₂ ≠ [] ∧
960removed s₁.length + s₂.length ≤ pumpingConstant re ∧
961removed ∀ m, s₁ ++ napp m s₂ ++ s₃ =~ re := by
962removed sorry
963removed
964removedend Pumping
965removedend RegExp

1removedimport LF.SFLCompat
2removed
3removed-- # Basics: Functional Programming in Lean
4removed
5removed-- Note to developers (Jonathan Chan @ionathanch):
6removed-- [BCP: Old comment -- might be out of date?] There should
7removed-- be some instruction on interaction with the IDE, namely:
8removed--
9removed-- - how to read the proof state
10removed--
11removed-- - clicking immediately after a tactic will show you what
12removed-- it changed
13removed--
14removed-- - clicking after each `h` in `rw [h₁, h₂, ...]` will show
15removed-- you what was rewritten
16removed--
17removed-- - hovering over a tactic will provide documentation on how
18removed-- to use it
19removed--
20removed-- - hovering over a definition will give its type
21removed--
22removed-- - hovering over a Unicode character will tell you how to
23removed-- type it
24removed--
25removed-- - Ctrl-clicking on a definition will take you to the
26removed-- definition location
27removed
28removed-- ## Data and Functions
29removed
30removed-- In Lean, we can build practically everything from first
31removed-- principles...
32removed
33removed-- ### Days of the Week (Enumerated Types)
34removed
35removed-- A datatype definition:
36removed
37removedinductive Day : Type where
38removed | monday
39removed | tuesday
40removed | wednesday
41removed | thursday
42removed | friday
43removed | saturday
44removed | sunday
45removed
46removed-- A function on days:
47removed
48removeddef nextWorkingDay (d : Day) : Day :=
49removed match d with
50removed | Day.monday => Day.tuesday
51removed | Day.tuesday => Day.wednesday
52removed | Day.wednesday => Day.thursday
53removed | Day.thursday => Day.friday
54removed | Day.friday => Day.monday
55removed | Day.saturday => Day.monday
56removed | Day.sunday => Day.monday
57removed
58removed-- Evaluation:
59removed
60removed#eval nextWorkingDay Day.friday
61removed
62removed#eval nextWorkingDay (nextWorkingDay Day.saturday)
63removed
64removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
65removed-- Where are we showing responses in comments? I don't see
66removed-- them. MWH: I think we landed at three possibilities:
67removed--
68removed-- 1. Don't include them
69removed--
70removed-- 2. Include responses in comments
71removed--
72removed-- 3. Use `#guard_msgs(...)` to include the responses and also
73removed-- check that they are correct. I vote that we do the last
74removed-- of these. It's useful for quietening the build, for
75removed-- helping readers be sure that things are working as
76removed-- expected, and for keeping things up to date.
77removed--
78removed-- Also: Further down in the text it says you can hover
79removed-- over the definitions to see their output. This is not
80removed-- happening in the web interface; it just shows the type
81removed-- of `#eval` and the types of the arguments, not the
82removed-- "message" it produces.
83removed
84removed-- We can also record what we *expect* the result of calling a
85removed-- function to be in the form of a Lean `example`:
86removed
87removedexample : nextWorkingDay (nextWorkingDay Day.saturday) = Day.tuesday := by
88removed rfl
89removed
90removed-- The `rfl` tactic is used to observe that both sides of an
91removed-- equal sign evaluate to the same value.
92removed
93removed-- ### Booleans
94removed
95removed-- Another familiar enumerated type; we'll switch to Lean's
96removed-- built-in `Bool` later:
97removed
98removedinductive MyBool : Type where
99removed | true
100removed | false
101removed
102removed-- This command opens the namespace associated with the
103removed-- `MyBool` type:
104removed
105removednamespace MyBool
106removed
107removed-- Functions over booleans can be defined in the same way as
108removed-- functions over days of the week.
109removed
110removeddef not (b : MyBool) : MyBool :=
111removed match b with
112removed | MyBool.true => MyBool.false
113removed | MyBool.false => MyBool.true
114removed
115removeddef and (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool) : MyBool :=
116removed match b1 with
117removed | MyBool.true => b2
118removed | MyBool.false => MyBool.false
119removed
120removeddef or (b1 : MyBool) (b2 : MyBool) : MyBool :=
121removed match b1 with
122removed | MyBool.true => MyBool.true
123removed | MyBool.false => b2
124removed
125removed-- Note the syntax for defining multi-argument functions (`and`
126removed-- and `or`).
127removed
128removedexample : or MyBool.true MyBool.false = MyBool.true := by rfl
129removedexample : or MyBool.false MyBool.false = MyBool.false := by rfl
130removedexample : or MyBool.false MyBool.true = MyBool.true := by rfl
131removedexample : or MyBool.true MyBool.true = MyBool.true := by rfl
132removed
133removed-- We can define new symbolic notations for existing
134removed-- definitions. Don't worry for now about how the notation is
135removed-- defined.
136removed
137removedlocal prefix:40 (priority := high) "!" => not
138removedlocal infixl:35 (priority := high) " && " => and
139removedlocal infixl:30 (priority := high) " || " => or
140removed
141removedexample : (MyBool.false || MyBool.false || MyBool.true) = MyBool.true := by rfl
142removed
143removedexample : (!MyBool.false) = MyBool.true := by rfl

180removed-- ### Basic Proofs
181removed
182removed-- Let's prove something simple about booleans:
183removed
184removedtheorem true_and : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b := by
185removed intro b
186removed rfl
187removed
188removed-- And now let's see it in a bit more detail:
189removed
190removed-- Note to developers (mwhicks1):
191removed-- The theorem below has wonderful explaining what's going
192removed-- on, but it is not typeset. Are we planning to fix that
193removed-- problem? I re-flowed the text so it reads better on the
194removed-- WWW in case not.
195removed
196removedtheorem true_and_explained : ∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b := by
197removed /- Move your cursor (click) here to see the initial proof state in
198removed the InfoView. The context (before the ⊢) is empty.
199removed The goal is `∀ (b : MyBool), (MyBool.true && b) = b`. -/
200removed intro b
201removed /- Now click here to see the new proof state that results from the
202removed tactic. Notice how `intro b` has changed the _context_: it now
203removed contains `b : MyBool`.
204removed
205removed The `intro` tactic is used to name variables quantified by a `∀`.
206removed Since we are trying to prove a property of all `MyBools`, we
207removed proceed by introducing an unknown `MyBool` `b` and prove
208removed the property holds for `b`, regardless of what it is. Informally,
209removed this move can be read, "We want to prove <some property> for all
210removed `MyBool`s `b`. So suppose `b` is some arbitrary `MyBool`...
211removed <and then go on to prove the property for this particular `b`>..."
212removed Since `b` was chosen arbitrarily, we've now proved the property
213removed for all `b`.
214removed
215removed A proof of a theorem beginning with a ∀ will typically start with
216removed an `intro`.
217removed
218removed As in the `example`s above, we can use the `rfl` tactic,
219removed which closes goals about equality where both sides are equal to
220removed one another according to the principle of reflexivity. Now,
221removed inspecting our goal will show that it is `(MyBool.true && b) = b`,
222removed which may not appear to be equal to itself. However, the tactic
223removed _evaluates_ both sides of the equality before comparing them. In
224removed this case, if we look at the definition of `and`, we can see that,
225removed when its first argument is `MyBool.true`, the result is its second
226removed argument. So the two terms `MyBool.true && b` and `b` are in fact
227removed equal because one evaluates to the other.
228removed -/
229removed rfl
230removed /- The proof is now done! The Lean InfoView tells us there are "No goals". -/
231removed

278removed | Color.black => Bool.true

283removed-- don't care about:

287removed | Color.black => Bool.true

292removed-- specific primary color:

294removeddef isRed (c : Color) : Bool :=
295removed match c with
296removed | Color.black => Bool.false
297removed | Color.white => Bool.false
298removed | Color.primary RGB.red => Bool.true
299removed | Color.primary _ => Bool.false

302removed-- explicitly nest match statements:
303removed
304removeddef isRed' (c : Color) : Bool :=
305removed match c with
306removed | Color.black => Bool.false
307removed | Color.white => Bool.false
308removed | Color.primary r =>
309removed match r with
310removed | RGB.red => Bool.true
311removed | _ => Bool.false

357removed-- `namespace` declarations create separate namespaces.

409removed | monday => tuesday
410removed | tuesday => wednesday
411removed | wednesday => thursday
412removed | thursday => friday

414removed | saturday => monday
415removed | sunday => monday

418removed
419removednamespace MyNamespace

421removedend MyNamespace

423removedopen MyNamespace

427removed-- If we only want to bring *some*, rather than all, of the
428removed-- definitions of a namespace into the current scope, we can
429removed-- use the `open (...)` form:
430removed
431removednamespace MyOtherNamespace

433removeddef myVisibleDef : Bool := Bool.false
434removedend MyOtherNamespace

444removedsf_expect_failure

448removed-- available without qualification.

459removed | .tuesday => .wednesday

493removed-- ### Constructors with Multiple Parameters (Tuple Types)
494removed
495removednamespace Playground
496removed
497removed-- A Nibble is half a byte -- four bits.
498removed
499removedinductive Bit : Type where
500removed | b1
501removed | b0
502removed
503removedinductive Nibble : Type where
504removed | bits (x0 x1 x2 x3 : Bit)
505removed
506removed#check (.bits .b1 .b0 .b1 .b0 : Nibble)
507removed
508removed-- We can deconstruct a Nibble by pattern-matching.
509removed
510removeddef allZero (nb : Nibble) : Bool :=
511removed match nb with
512removed | .bits .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0 => true
513removed | .bits _ _ _ _ => false
514removed
515removedexample : allZero (.bits .b1 .b0 .b1 .b0) = false := by rfl
516removedexample : allZero (.bits .b0 .b0 .b0 .b0) = true := by rfl
517removed
518removedend Playground
519removed
520removed-- ### Natural Numbers
521removed
522removednamespace NatPlayground
523removed
524removed-- For simplicity in proofs, we choose a *unary* representation
525removed-- of natural numbers.
526removed
527removedinductive Nat : Type where
528removed | zero
529removed | succ (n : Nat)
530removed
531removed-- Eventually we'll swap to Lean's definition of natural
532removed-- numbers, which is very similar to this.
533removed
534removednamespace Nat
535removed
536removeddef one : Nat := succ zero
537removeddef two : Nat := succ one
538removeddef three : Nat := succ two
539removeddef four : Nat := succ three
540removed
541removed-- We can also write functions on `Nat`.
542removed
543removeddef pred (n : Nat) : Nat :=
544removed match n with
545removed | zero => zero
546removed | succ n' => n'
547removed
548removeddef minustwo (n : Nat) : Nat :=
549removed match n with
550removed | zero => zero
551removed | succ (zero) => zero
552removed | succ (succ n') => n'
553removed
554removed#eval minustwo four
555removed
556removed-- Here are some recursive functions on natural numbers:
557removed
558removeddef even (n : Nat) : Bool :=
559removed match n with
560removed | zero => true
561removed | succ (zero) => false
562removed | succ (succ n') => even n'
563removed
564removedexample : even one = false := by rfl
565removedexample : even four = true := by rfl
566removed
567removed-- We could define `odd` by a similar recursive declaration,
568removed-- but here is a simpler way:
569removed
570removeddef odd (n : Nat) : Bool :=
571removed not (even n)
572removed
573removedexample : odd one = true := by rfl
574removedexample : odd four = false := by rfl
575removed
576removed-- This function takes multiple parameters, recursing on the
577removed-- second:
578removed
579removeddef add (n : Nat) (m : Nat) : Nat :=
580removed match m with
581removed | zero => n
582removed | succ m' => succ (add n m')
583removed
584removed#eval add one two -- succ (succ (succ zero)) -- aka, three!
585removed
586removed-- We can also define infix notation for our `add` functions.
587removed
588removedscoped infixl:65 " + " => add
589removed
590removed#eval one + two -- succ (succ (succ zero)) -- aka, three again.
591removed
592removed-- ## Proof by Rewriting
593removed
594removed-- ### Proving properties about functions in Lean
595removed
596removed-- We can prove properties of recursive functions like `add`:
597removed
598removedtheorem add_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero = n := by
599removed intro n
600removed rfl
601removed
602removed#check add_zero
603removed
604removed-- Using our simplification rule `add_zero`, we can carry out a
605removed-- simple proof about natural numbers!
606removed
607removedtheorem add_zero_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero + zero = n := by
608removed intro n
609removed rewrite [add_zero]
610removed rewrite [add_zero]
611removed rfl
612removed
613removed-- We'll walk through this proof in the next section.
614removed
615removed-- ### Proof state and tactics
616removed
617removed-- Here is the previous proof in more detail:
618removed
619removedtheorem add_zero_zero_explained : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero + zero = n := by
620removed intro n
621removed /- After introducing `n`, our goal is `n + zero + zero = n`.
622removed What can we do to simplify this expression? If you hover your cursor over the
623removed `add_zero` in the rewrite below, you can see its type: `n + zero = n`. So,
624removed we can use that rewrite rule to transform an appearnce of `n + zero` in the goal to `n`. -/
625removed rewrite [add_zero]
626removed /- Now click here to see the new proof state that results from the tactic.
627removed Notice how `n + zero + zero` changes to `n + zero` in the goal. -/
628removed rewrite [add_zero]
629removed /- Again the goal changes, from `n + zero` to `n`. Now the proof state
630removed is an equality with both sides equal, so it can be closed by the
631removed tactic `rfl`. -/
632removed rfl
633removed /- The proof is now done! The Lean InfoView tells us there are "No goals". -/
634removed
635removed-- Give this proof a try (it's similar):
636removed
637removedtheorem add_zero_zero_zero : ∀ n : Nat, n + zero + zero + zero = n := by
638removed sorry
639removed
640removed-- The `rfl` closes a goal that looks like `a = a`, reducing
641removed-- both sides of the equality in the process.
642removed
643removed-- ### A New `add` Rule
644removed
645removed-- Here's another rule we can use for `add`:
646removed
647removedtheorem add_succ : ∀ n m : Nat, n + (succ m) = succ (n + m) := by
648removed intro n m
649removed rfl
650removed
651removed-- Now, let's use `add_succ` in a proof:
652removed
653removedtheorem add_one (n : Nat) : n + (succ zero) = succ n + zero := by
654removed rewrite [add_succ]
655removed rewrite [add_zero]
656removed rewrite [add_zero]
657removed rfl
658removed
659removed-- ### Irreducibility, Rewriting, and Proof Engineering
660removed
661removed-- After proving the theorems that characterize a definition,
662removed-- we mark the definition `irreducible` to require rewriting by
663removed-- them instead of using `rfl`.
664removed
665removedattribute [irreducible] add
666removed
667removed-- These characterizing theorems also follow a particular
668removed-- pattern. Let's look again at the definition of `add`,
669removed-- without the `+` notation for maximum clarity:
670removed
671removednamespace AddPlayground
672removed
673removeddef add (n : Nat) (m : Nat) : Nat :=
674removed match m with
675removed | zero => n
676removed | succ m' => succ (add n m')
677removed
678removedtheorem add_zero : ∀ (n : Nat), add n zero = n := by
679removed intro n
680removed rfl
681removed
682removedtheorem add_succ : ∀ (n m : Nat), add n (succ m) = succ (add n m) := by
683removed intro n m
684removed rfl
685removed
686removedend AddPlayground
687removed
688removed-- Each branch of a definition's control flow gets one
689removed-- *simplification lemma*. Here are the two for `pred`:
690removed
691removedtheorem pred_zero : pred zero = zero := by rfl
692removedtheorem pred_succ n : pred (succ n) = n := by rfl
693removed
694removed-- Now that we have defined and proved `pred`'s simplification
695removed-- lemmas, we can mark it `irreducible`, to enforce rewriting
696removed-- by these lemmas.
697removed
698removedattribute [irreducible] pred
699removed
700removed-- Similarly, for each of the three branches of the definition
701removed-- of `even`, we need one simplification lemma:
702removed
703removedtheorem even_zero : even zero = true := rfl
704removedtheorem even_one : even (succ zero) = false := rfl
705removedtheorem even_succ_succ n : even (succ (succ n)) = even n := rfl
706removed
707removedattribute [irreducible] even odd
708removed
709removed-- From here on, we pair each definition with its
710removed-- simplification lemmas and rewrite by those lemmas rather
711removed-- than `rfl`-ing through the definition.
712removed
713removed-- ### Working with Numerals
714removed
715removed-- We know from our definitions above that `one` is just
716removed-- `succ zero`, `two` is `succ one`, and so on. We can write
717removed-- rules for these equalities too:
718removed
719removedtheorem one_eq_succ_zero : one = succ zero := by rfl
720removedtheorem two_eq_succ_one : two = succ one := by rfl
721removedtheorem three_eq_succ_two : three = succ two := by rfl
722removedtheorem four_eq_succ_three : four = succ three := by rfl
723removed
724removed-- Finish the proof using the `add` rules:
725removed
726removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
727removed-- Should this be marked / formatted as an exercise or at
728removed-- least a WORKINCLASS? RAB: Let's decide once we choose
729removed-- how to present the laws. My intuition is yes.
730removed
731removedtheorem one_plus_one_eq_two : (one + one : Nat) = two := by
732removed rewrite [one_eq_succ_zero]
733removed sorry
734removed
735removed-- Try the same for `two + two = four`.
736removed
737removedtheorem two_plus_two_eq_four : two + two = four := by
738removed sorry
739removed
740removeddef mul (n m : Nat) : Nat :=
741removed match m with
742removed | zero => zero
743removed | succ m' => (mul n m') + n
744removed
745removedscoped infixl:70 " * " => mul
746removed
747removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): mul_simpl_rules ⭐
748removed
749removed-- Multiplication, like any function we will prove properties
750removed-- about, also has simplification rules.
751removed
752removed-- Remove `sorry` and prove the simplification rules for `mul`
753removed-- below. You will likely find the proofs of the simplification
754removed-- rules for `add` to be helpful as a model.

774removed rewrite [one_eq_succ_zero]
775removed sorry
776removed

779removed sorry
780removed
781removed

783removed rewrite [two_eq_succ_one, one_eq_succ_zero]
784removed sorry

787removed rewrite [two_eq_succ_one, one_eq_succ_zero]

794removed-- Here is a function `beq` that tests natural numbers for
795removed-- equality, yielding a boolean.
796removed
797removeddef beq (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
798removed match n with
799removed | zero => match m with
800removed | zero => true
801removed | succ _ => false
802removed | succ n' => match m with
803removed | zero => false
804removed | succ m' => beq n' m'
805removed
806removed-- We could also write this by pattern matching on both `n` and
807removed-- `m` at the same time:
808removed
809removeddef beq' (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
810removed match n, m with
811removed | zero, zero => true
812removed | zero, succ _ => false
813removed | succ _, zero => false
814removed | succ n', succ m' => beq n' m'
815removed
816removed-- The definitions of `beq` and `beq'` are equivalent.
817removed
818removed-- Similarly, the `ble` function tests whether its first
819removed-- argument is less than or equal to its second argument,
820removed-- yielding a boolean.
821removed
822removeddef ble (n m : Nat) : Bool :=
823removed match n with
824removed | zero => true
825removed | succ n' =>
826removed match m with
827removed | zero => false
828removed | succ m' => ble n' m'
829removed
830removedtheorem zero_ble (n : Nat) : ble zero n = true := by rfl
831removedtheorem succ_ble_zero (n : Nat) : ble (succ n) zero = false := by rfl
832removedtheorem succ_ble_succ (n m : Nat) : ble (succ n) (succ m) = ble n m := by rfl
833removed
834removedexample : ble two two = true := by rfl
835removedexample : ble two four = true := by rfl
836removedexample : ble four two = false := by rfl
837removed

843removed := sorry
844removed
845removedexample : blt two two = false := sorry
846removedexample : blt two four = true := sorry
847removedexample : blt four two = false := sorry
848removed
849removedattribute [irreducible] blt ble
850removed
851removed-- We'll be using `beq` a lot, so let's give it an infix
852removed-- notation.
853removed
854removedscoped infixl:30 " == " => beq
855removed
856removed-- Note that now `==` and `=` are different; the former means
857removed-- `beq` whereas the latter is a logical claim.
858removed
859removedtheorem zero_zero_beq_true : (zero == zero) = true := by rfl
860removedtheorem zero_succ_beq_false (n : Nat) : (zero == (succ n)) = false := by rfl
861removedtheorem succ_zero_beq_false (n : Nat) : ((succ n) == zero) = false := by rfl
862removedtheorem succ_succ_beq (n m : Nat) : ((succ n) == (succ m)) = (n == m) := by rfl
863removed
864removedattribute [irreducible] beq

909removed-- ## Proof by Case Analysis
910removed
911removed-- Sometimes simple calculation and rewriting are not enough...
912removed
913removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
914removed-- At the moment our convention for unfinished proofs is to
915removed-- end with sorry and guard the "proof uses sorry" warning.
916removed-- However after going through MRC's comments here I
917removed-- realized we don't need to do this: we can leave the
918removed-- proof unfinished and guard the error about goals being
919removed-- unsolved. IMO this is preferable because it illustrates
920removed-- more directly what is going on.
921removed--
922removed-- However, before we can do this, I think we may require a
923removed-- minor change to how Verso files get compiled to Lean. If
924removed-- we just naïvely strip out #guard msgs, the generated
925removed-- .lean files will now have errors since those commands
926removed-- were guarding actual errors rather than just warnings.
927removed-- So we would need a way to have .lean files with errors
928removed-- in them permitted by the make command, or we would need
929removed-- to leave in #guard msgs that are guarding actual errors.
930removed--
931removed-- BCP: This is a tricky balancing act!! Let's talk about
932removed-- it.
933removed--
934removed-- `/--
935removed-- error: unsolved goals
936removed-- n : Nat
937removed-- ⊢ (succ n == zero) = false
938removed-- -/
939removed-- #guard_msgs(error) in
940removed-- example : ∀ n : Nat,
941removed-- (succ n == zero) = false := by
942removed-- intro n
943removed-- /-
944removed-- We can't rewrite by any lemmas here because `n` is unknown!
945removed-- -/`
946removed
947removedexample : ∀ n : Nat,
948removed (succ n == zero) = false := by
949removed intro n
950removed /-
951removed We can't rewrite by any lemmas here because `n` is unknown!
952removed -/
953removed sorry
954removed
955removed-- We can use `cases` to perform case analysis:
956removed
957removedtheorem add_one_neb_zero : ∀ n : Nat,
958removed (succ n == zero) = false := by
959removed intro n
960removed cases n
961removed case zero =>
962removed rewrite [succ_zero_beq_false]
963removed rfl
964removed case succ n' =>
965removed rewrite [succ_zero_beq_false]
966removed rfl
967removed
968removed-- Another example, using booleans:
969removed
970removedtheorem not_involutive : ∀ b : Bool, (!!b) = b := by
971removed intro b
972removed cases b
973removed case false =>
974removed rewrite [Bool.not_false, Bool.not_true]
975removed rfl
976removed case true =>
977removed rewrite [Bool.not_true, Bool.not_false]
978removed rfl
979removed
980removed-- Some of the above proofs use standard library lemmas; later
981removed-- on we will discuss how to search for those yourself.
982removed
983removed-- We can also have nested case analysis:
984removed
985removedtheorem and_commutative : ∀ b c : Bool,
986removed (b && c) = (c && b) := by
987removed intro b c
988removed cases b
989removed case true =>
990removed cases c
991removed case true =>
992removed rewrite [Bool.and_self]
993removed rfl
994removed case false =>
995removed rewrite [Bool.and_false, Bool.and_true]
996removed rfl
997removed case false =>
998removed cases c
999removed case true =>
1000removed rewrite [Bool.and_true, Bool.and_false]
1001removed rfl
1002removed case false =>
1003removed rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1004removed rfl
1005removed
1006removedtheorem and3_exchange : ∀ b c d : Bool,
1007removed ((b && c) && d) = ((b && d) && c) := by
1008removed intro b c d
1009removed cases b
1010removed case false =>
1011removed cases c
1012removed case true =>
1013removed cases d
1014removed case false =>
1015removed rewrite [Bool.and_true, Bool.and_self]
1016removed rfl
1017removed case true =>
1018removed rewrite [Bool.and_true]
1019removed rfl
1020removed case false =>
1021removed cases d
1022removed case false =>
1023removed rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1024removed rfl
1025removed case true =>
1026removed rewrite [Bool.and_self, Bool.and_true]
1027removed rfl
1028removed case true =>
1029removed cases c
1030removed case true =>
1031removed cases d
1032removed case false =>
1033removed rewrite [Bool.and_self, Bool.and_false, Bool.and_true]
1034removed rfl
1035removed case true =>
1036removed rewrite [Bool.and_self]
1037removed rfl
1038removed case false =>
1039removed cases d
1040removed case false =>
1041removed rewrite [Bool.and_false]
1042removed rfl
1043removed case true =>
1044removed rewrite [Bool.and_false, Bool.and_true, Bool.and_self]
1045removed rfl
1046removed
1047removed-- As you can see, proofs by cases can become very verbose. We
1048removed-- will introduce some tactics for writing shorter proofs by
1049removed-- case analysis in `Tactics.lean`.
1050removed

1096removed-- ### Binary Numerals
1097removed
1098removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): binary ⭐⭐⭐
1099removed
1100removed-- We can generalize our unary representation of natural
1101removed-- numbers to the more efficient binary representation by
1102removed-- treating a binary number as a sequence of constructors `b0`
1103removed-- and `b1` (representing 0s and 1s), terminated by a `z`.
1104removed
1105removed-- For example:
1106removed
1107removed-- decimal binary unary
1108removed-- 0 z zero
1109removed-- 1 b1 z succ zero
1110removed-- 2 b0 (b1 z) succ (succ zero)
1111removed-- 3 b1 (b1 z) succ (succ (succ zero))
1112removed-- 4 b0 (b0 (b1 z)) succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))
1113removed-- 5 b1 (b0 (b1 z)) succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero))))
1114removed-- 6 b0 (b1 (b1 z)) succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))))
1115removed-- 7 b1 (b1 (b1 z)) succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero))))))
1116removed-- 8 b0 (b0 (b0 (b1 z))) succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))))))
1117removed
1118removed-- Note that the low-order bit is on the left and the
1119removed-- high-order bit is on the right -- the opposite of the way
1120removed-- binary numbers are usually written. This choice makes them
1121removed-- easier to manipulate.
1122removed
1123removed-- (Comprehension check: What unary numeral does `b0 z`
1124removed-- represent?)
1125removed
1126removedinductive Bin : Type where
1127removed | z
1128removed | b0 (n : Bin)
1129removed | b1 (n : Bin)
1130removed
1131removedattribute [pp_nodot] Bin.b1 Bin.b0
1132removed
1133removeddef incr (m : Bin) : Bin
1134removed := sorry
1135removed
1136removeddef binToNat (m : Bin) : Nat
1137removed := sorry
1138removed
1139removedexample : incr (.b1 .z) = .b0 (.b1 .z) := sorry
1140removedexample : incr (.b0 (.b1 .z)) = .b1 (.b1 .z) := sorry
1141removedexample : incr (.b1 (.b1 .z)) = .b0 (.b0 (.b1 .z)) := sorry
1142removed
1143removedtheorem incr_z : incr .z = .b1 .z := sorry
1144removedtheorem incr_b0 m : incr (.b0 m) = .b1 m := sorry
1145removedtheorem incr_b1 m : incr (.b1 m) = .b0 (incr m) := sorry
1146removed
1147removedtheorem binToNat_z : binToNat .z = zero := sorry
1148removedtheorem binToNat_b0 m : binToNat (.b0 m) = binToNat m * two := sorry
1149removedtheorem binToNat_b1 m : binToNat (.b1 m) = binToNat m * two + one := sorry
1150removed
1151removed-- You may find your previous proofs of `zero_add_one`,
1152removed-- `one_add_one`, `zero_mul_two`, `one_mul_two`, and
1153removed-- `two_mul_two` useful here.
1154removed
1155removedexample : binToNat (.b0 (.b1 .z)) = two := sorry
1156removedexample : binToNat (incr (.b1 .z)) = add one (binToNat (.b1 .z)) := sorry
1157removedexample : binToNat (incr (incr (.b1 .z))) = add two (binToNat (.b1 .z)) := sorry
1158removedexample : binToNat (.b0 (.b0 (.b1 .z))) = four := sorry
1159removed
1160removedattribute [irreducible] incr binToNat
1161removed
1162removedend Nat

1253removed | A, _ => gt
1254removed | B, A => lt
1255removed | B, B => eq
1256removed | B, _ => gt
1257removed | C, A => lt
1258removed | C, B => lt

1260removed | C, _ => gt
1261removed | D, F => gt
1262removed | D, D => eq
1263removed | D, _ => lt
1264removed | F, F => eq
1265removed | F, _ => lt

1338removedexample : lowerGrade (lowerGrade (lowerGrade ⟨B, minus⟩)) = ⟨C, minus⟩ := sorry

1340removedtheorem lowerGrade_F_Minus : lowerGrade ⟨F, minus⟩ = ⟨F, minus⟩ := sorry

1342removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): lower_grade_lowers ⭐⭐⭐
1343removed
1344removed-- Note to developers:
1345removed-- For our solution we use:
1346removed--
1347removed-- - Working on multiple match cases with
1348removed-- `| _ ... | _ => ...`;
1349removed--
1350removed-- - Working on all remaining goals with `all_goals`.
1351removed--
1352removed-- - These are not expected of students at this point.
1353removed
1354removedtheorem lowerGrade_lowers : ∀ g : Grade,
1355removed gradeComparison ⟨F, minus⟩ g = lt →
1356removed gradeComparison (lowerGrade g) g = lt := by
1357removed sorry
1358removed
1359removed-- Note to developers (Roger Burtonpatel @rogerburtonpatel):
1360removed-- in removing `dsimp` from these proofs, I found that you
1361removed-- might need the `contradiction` tactic here instead, or
1362removed-- some other reasoning that's not accomplishable with the
1363removed-- tactics we've introduced so far. Can you make this proof
1364removed-- work with only `rw`, `rfl`, `exact`, etc?
1365removed
1366removeddef applyLatePolicy (lateDays : NatPlayground.Nat) (g : Grade) : Grade :=
1367removed if Nat.ble lateDays 9 then g
1368removed else if Nat.ble lateDays 17 then lowerGrade g
1369removed else if Nat.ble lateDays 21 then lowerGrade (lowerGrade g)
1370removed else lowerGrade (lowerGrade (lowerGrade g))
1371removed
1372removedtheorem applyLatePolicy_unfold : ∀ (lateDays : NatPlayground.Nat) (g : Grade),
1373removed applyLatePolicy lateDays g
1374removed =
1375removed (if Nat.ble lateDays 9 then g
1376removed else if Nat.ble lateDays 17 then lowerGrade g
1377removed else if Nat.ble lateDays 21 then lowerGrade (lowerGrade g)
1378removed else lowerGrade (lowerGrade (lowerGrade g))) := by
1379removed intro _ _; rfl
1380removed
1381removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): no_penalty_for_mostly_on_time ⭐⭐
1382removed
1383removedtheorem no_penalty_for_mostly_on_time : ∀ (lateDays : NatPlayground.Nat) (g : Grade),
1384removed (Nat.ble lateDays 9 = true) →
1385removed applyLatePolicy lateDays g = g := by
1386removed sorry
1387removed
1388removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): grade_lowered_once ⭐⭐
1389removed
1390removedtheorem grade_lowered_once : ∀ (lateDays : NatPlayground.Nat) (g : Grade),
1391removed (Nat.ble lateDays 9 = false) →
1392removed (Nat.ble lateDays 17 = true) →
1393removed applyLatePolicy lateDays g = lowerGrade g := by
1394removed sorry
1395removed
1396removedend LateDays
1397removed

30removed/--
31removed `inversion t` generalizes nonvariable indices of the type of `t` before invoking `cases t`,

34removed if trying to generalize the indices produces an ill-typed result.

37removed * The form `inversion t with | tag₁ x ... => tac ... | ... | tagₙ z ... => tac ...` is supported,
38removed similar to that of `cases` and `inversion`.

47removed/--
48removed This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
49removed form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
50removed each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
51removed and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
52removed It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
53removed
54removed This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
55removed - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
56removed - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
57removed - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
58removed
59removed Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
60removed-/
61removeddef forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
62removed (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
63removed MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
64removed let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
65removed unless ms.size == 1 do
66removed if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
67removed else throwError m!"Failed"
68removed let mut mvs := ms
69removed let mut bis := bs
70removed let mut out : Expr := tp
71removed while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
72removed let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
73removed unless ms.size == 1 do
74removed throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
75removed mvs := mvs ++ ms
76removed bis := bis ++ bs
77removed out := tp
78removed return (mvs, bis, out)
79removed
80removed/-- Get the user-facing name for the given metavariable. -/
81removeddef _root_.Lean.MVarId.getUserName (mvarId : MVarId) : MetaM Name := do
82removed let decl ← mvarId.getDecl
83removed return decl.userName
84removed
85removed/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
86removed unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
87removed but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
88removed This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
89removed While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
90removed decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
91removed
92removed Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
93removedpartial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
94removed match eqs with
95removed | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
96removed | eq :: eqs =>
97removed let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
98removed | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
99removed let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
100removed let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
101removed unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
102removed
103removed/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
104removeddef unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
105removed subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
106removed let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
107removed let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
108removed if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
109removed else return some { s with
110removed mvarId := mvarId,
111removed subst := subst,
112removed fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
113removed }
114removed
115removed/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
116removed using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
117removed
118removed As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context. -/
119removeddef casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
120removed subgoals.mapM fun s => do
121removed let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
122removed let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
123removed return { s with mvarId }
124removed
125removedend Lean.Meta

130removed-- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
131removed-- [https://github.com/leanprover-community/batteries/blob/main/Batteries/Tactic/Lemma.lean]
132removed/-- Synonym for `theorem`. -/
133removedmacro "lemma " thm:declId sig:declSig val:declVal : command => `(theorem $thm $sig $val)
134removed
135removed/--
136removed `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
137removed Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
138removed metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
139removed then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
140removed original `i`.
141removed
142removed Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/ApplyAt.lean].
143removed-/
144removedelab "apply " t:term " at " i:ident : tactic => withSynthesize <| withMainContext do
145removed let f ← elabTermForApply t
146removed let some ldecl := (← getLCtx).findFromUserName? i.getId
147removed | throwErrorAt i m!"Identifier {i} not found"
148removed let (mvs, bis, _) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq (← inferType f) ldecl.type
149removed for (m, b) in mvs.zip bis do
150removed if b.isInstImplicit && !(← m.mvarId!.isAssigned) then
151removed try m.mvarId!.inferInstance
152removed catch _ => continue
153removed let (_, mainGoal) ← (← getMainGoal).note ldecl.userName
154removed (← mkAppOptM' f (mvs.pop.push ldecl.toExpr |>.map some))
155removed let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId
156removed replaceMainGoal <| [mainGoal] ++ mvs.pop.toList.map (·.mvarId!)
157removed
158removedstructure InversionConfig where
159removed clear : Bool := false
160removed
161removeddeclare_config_elab elabInversionConfig InversionConfig
162removed
163removedopen Cases in
164removeddef inversionCore (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig) : TacticM (List CasesSubgoal) := withMainContext do
165removed let goal ← getMainGoal
166removed goal.withContext do
167removed let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
168removed | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
169removed -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
170removed if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
171removed let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h default ctx
172removed let subgoals ← if config.clear
173removed then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
174removed else pure subgoals
175removed return subgoals.toList
176removed -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
177removed else
178removed let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
179removed let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
180removed let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
181removed | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
182removed let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget default ctx
183removed let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
184removed let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
185removed let subgoals ← if config.clear
186removed then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
187removed else pure subgoals
188removed return subgoals.toList
189removed
190removed/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
191removed solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
192removed throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
193removeddef evalInvAlt (goals : List CasesSubgoal) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
194removed match alt with
195removed | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
196removed if let some goal := goals.find? (matchTag tag.getId $ ·.ctorName.getD default) then
197removed return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal.mvarId]
198removed else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
199removed | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
200removed if !goals.isEmpty then
201removed goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics ·.mvarId)
202removed else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
203removed | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
204removedwhere
205removed matchTag tag name : Bool :=
206removed tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
207removed trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
208removed let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
209removed unless goals.isEmpty do
210removed reportUnsolvedGoals goals
211removed return goal
212removed errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
213removed let goalMsgs := goals.filterMap (.ofName <$> ·.ctorName)
214removed return if goals.isEmpty
215removed then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
216removed else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
217removed
218removed@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
219removedpublic meta def evalInversion : Tactic
220removed | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
221removed let config ← elabInversionConfig config
222removed let mut goals ← inversionCore (← getFVarId h) config
223removed if let some alts := alts? then
224removed let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
225removed for alt in expandedAlts do
226removed let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
227removed goals := goals.filter (!solvedGoals.contains ·.mvarId)
228removed unless goals.isEmpty do
229removed reportUnsolvedGoals $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
230removed replaceMainGoal $ goals.map (·.mvarId)
231removed | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
232removedwhere expandInvAlts
233removed | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
234removed args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
235removed | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
236removed
237removedend Lean.Elab.Tactic
