1170removed-- to `true` or `false`; this only works for `Bool`, not
1171removed-- `Prop`.
1172removed
1173removed-- The third row highlights an important practical difference:
1174removed-- equality functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean
1175removed-- cannot be used directly to justify rewriting with the
1176removed-- rewrite tactic; propositional equality is required for this.
1177removed-- Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1178removed-- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a
1179removed-- property that happens to be decidable: we can express it
1180removed-- either as a boolean computation or as a function into Prop.
1181removed
1182removed-- As an example, we can write
1183removed
1184removedunseal isEven in
1185removedexample : isEven 42 := rfl
1186removed
1187removed-- or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
1188removed
1189removedunseal double in
1190removedexample : Even 42 := by exists 21
1191removed
1192removed-- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two
1193removed-- characterizations of evenness did not describe the same set
1194removed-- of natural numbers!
1195removed
1196removed-- Fortunately, they do! To prove this, we first need two
1197removed-- helper lemmas.
1198removed
1199removedtheorem even_double (k : Nat) : isEven (double k) = true := by
1200removed induction k with
1201removed | zero =>
1202removed rewrite [double_zero, isEven_zero]
1203removed rfl
1204removed | succ n ih =>
1205removed rewrite [double_succ, isEven_succ_succ]
1206removed exact ih
1207removed
1208removed-- ### Exercise (3 stars): isEven_double_exists ⭐⭐⭐
1209removed
1210removedtheorem isEven_double_exists (n : Nat) :
1211removed ∃ k, n = bif isEven n then double k else double k + 1 := by sorry
1212removed
1213removed-- Now the main theorem:
1214removed
1215removedtheorem isEven_iff_Even {n : Nat} : isEven n = true ↔ Even n where
1216removed mp h := by
1217removed have ⟨k, hk⟩ := isEven_double_exists n
1218removed rewrite [h, cond_true] at hk
1219removed subst hk
1220removed exists k
1221removed mpr h := by
1222removed obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h
1223removed subst hk
1224removed exact even_double k
1225removed
1226removed-- In view of this theorem, we can say that the boolean
1227removed-- computation `isEven n` is reflected in the truth of the
1228removed-- proposition `∃ k, n = double k`.
1229removed
1230removed-- Similarly, to state that two numbers n and m are equal, we
1231removed-- can say either
1232removed
1233removed-- - that `n == m` returns `true`, or
1234removed-- - that `n = m`
1235removed
1236removed-- Again, these two notions are equivalent:
1237removed
1238removed-- Note to developers:
1239removed-- This proof is from the typeclass version, which makes
1240removed-- more sense if maps are included — CGH
1241removed
1242removedexample (n₁ n₂ : Nat) : n₁ == n₂ ↔ n₁ = n₂ := beq_iff_eq
1243removed
1244removed-- So what should we do in situations where some claim could be
1245removed-- formalized as either a proposition or a boolean computation?
1246removed-- Which should we choose?
1247removed
1248removed-- In general, both can be useful. Which we choose has to do
1249removed-- with the *computational* nature of Lean's core language,
1250removed-- which is designed so that every function it expresses is
1251removed-- total, and by default computable unless we explicit indicate
1252removed-- otherwise. As an example, consider trying to write a
1253removed-- function `α → α → Bool` checking for equality on an
1254removed-- arbitrary type:
1255removed
1256removed-- Note to developers:
1257removed-- dsainati12 days ago We use regular if for the first time
1258removed-- here. It is probably necessary to explain at this point
1259removed-- what if is and how it differs from bif.
1260removed--
1261removed-- 👍 1 berberman1 day ago Should we clarify the difference
1262removed-- between = and ==? Observably if and bif can possibly
1263removed-- accept both as the condition because of Coe or
1264removed-- DecidableEq instances, which IMO could be confusing.
1265removed--
1266removed-- Probably we can talk a bit about the coercion system in
1267removed-- this file as well, since Coe could be an example of
1268removed-- typeclasses, so long as if we ignore the outParam
1269removed-- thing...
1270removed--
1271removed-- chenson20181 day ago I definitely intended for this to
1272removed-- cover = versus ==. Maps uses LawfulBEq (which says = and
1273removed-- == coincide). If that will now appear here it's a good
1274removed-- place to give some more detail?
1275removed--
1276removed-- rogerburtonpatel1 day ago I think right after this part
1277removed-- on decidability is good. It's a hefty chunk of
1278removed-- information already, so keeping distinct ideas distinct
1279removed-- is more likely than not a good call.
1280removed
1281removed-- Note to developers:
1282removed-- @dsainati - commenting this out for the same reason as
1283removed-- above
1284removed--
1285removed-- `def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) : Bool := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false`
1286removed
1287removed-- Lean will complain here that it cannot find an instance of
1288removed-- `Decidable`. This typeclass
1289removed
1290removed-- Note to developers:
1291removed-- @dsainati - commenting this out because the -keep
1292removed-- doesn't work during extraction; this causes Lean to get
1293removed-- the two instances (the real one and this one) confused
1294removed--
1295removed-- `class inductive Decidable (p : Prop) where
1296removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬p` -/
1297removed-- | isFalse (h : Not p) : Decidable p
1298removed-- /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p` -/
1299removed-- | isTrue (h : p) : Decidable p`
1300removed
1301removed-- is the way that we express in Lean that a given proposition
1302removed-- is decidable. This is the generalization of our observation
1303removed-- that `isEven_iff_Even` was reflecting a proof between
1304removed-- boolean and propositional equality. In fact, we can use this
1305removed-- theorem to directly construct a `Decidable` instance
1306removed
1307removedinstance (n : Nat) : Decidable (Even n) := decidable_of_decidable_of_iff isEven_iff_Even
1308removed
1309removed-- Now we are able to complete such proofs by computation using
1310removed-- the `decide` tactic:
1311removed
1312removedsection
1313removedunseal isEven
1314removed
1315removedexample : Even 2 := by decide
1316removedexample : Even 4 := by decide
1317removedexample : Even 6 := by decide
1318removedexample : Even 100 := by decide
1319removedexample : ¬ Even 101 := by decide
1320removedexample : ∀ n < 10, Even (2 * n) := by decide
1321removedexample : ∀ n < 10, Even (2 * n) ∧ ¬ Even (2 * n + 1) := by decide
1322removedend
1323removed
1324removed-- In general, Lean will try to use typeclass synthesis with
1325removed-- `Decidable` in order to determine when it is appropriate to
1326removed-- use `Prop` and `Bool` interchangeably. For instance, while
1327removed-- our example `eq` failed above while trying to use
1328removed-- propositional equality `=` in the condition of an `if`
1329removed-- statement, we are allowed to write
1330removed
1331removeddef nat_eq (m n : Nat) : Bool := if m = n then true else false
1332removed
1333removed-- Why is this allowed? It is precisely because equality of
1334removed-- natural numbers is decidable, and Lean makes use of this
1335removed-- fact. If we print this definition with notation unset, we
1336removed-- would find that it is using `instDecidableEqNat`
1337removed
1338removedset_option pp.all true in
1339removed#print nat_eq
1340removed
1341removed-- which proves that this equality is decidable.
1342removed
1343removed-- This is only half the story however: while Lean's core
1344removed-- theory enables this computation, Lean is also often used in
1345removed-- applications where we don't care about computability, such
1346removed-- as pure mathematics. In particular, it is possible to write
1347removed-- a function for arbitrary equality:
1348removed
1349removedsf_experiment
1350removed open scoped Classical in
1351removed noncomputable def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false
1352removed
1353removed set_option pp.all true in
1354removed #print eq
1355removed
1356removed-- But we have indicated to Lean, using the `noncomputable`
1357removed-- keyword and `Classical` namespace that we are *not*
1358removed-- interested in computation. What is happening in the
1359removed-- background is that this allows typeclass synthesis to find
1360removed-- the scoped instance `Classical.propDecidable`, which makes
1361removed-- use of the axiom of choice to provide a proof that all
1362removed-- propositions are *classically* decidable. This sort of
1363removed-- definition is suitable for use with proofs, but is not
1364removed-- allowed to be used in conjunction with computational
1365removed-- features of Lean such as the `decide` tactic or the `#eval`
1366removed-- command.
1367removed
1368removed-- ## TODO
1369removed
1370removed-- Note to developers:
1371removed-- Below are some stray examples from IndProp. `Decidable`
1372removed-- only carries the proposition and not the boolean, so one
1373removed-- direction of `reflect_iff` is easily translated, but the
1374removed-- other is a bit different. I list some theorems below but
1375removed-- you should Loogle and see if that's what you want. Some
1376removed-- the the proofs can be a bit advanced if you follow core,
1377removed-- or otherwise a bit circular. — CGH
1378removed
1379removed#check decidable_of_bool
1380removed
1381removedexample {P : Prop} (b : Bool) (h : b = true ↔ P) : Decidable P := by
1382removed by_cases hb : b
1383removed · apply isTrue
1384removed simp [← h, hb]
1385removed · apply isFalse
1386removed simp [← h, hb]
1387removed
1388removed#check decide_eq_false_iff_not
1389removed#check decide_eq_true_iff
1390removed
1391removed-- Note to developers:
1392removed-- I'm not sure what part of the signature here is
1393removed-- important to translate. Is the point the `Bool`/`Prop`
1394removed-- mismatch? — CGH
1395removed
1396removedexample (a : α) [BEq α] [LawfulBEq α] (xs : List α) (neq : xs.filter (a == ·) ≠ []) : a ∈ xs := by
1397removed sorry
1398removed

6removed-- # UsingLean: Using the full power of a proof assistant
7removed
8removed-- Note to developers (NOW):
9removed-- Chapter goals: Nats dsimp calc
10removed
11removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, NOW):
12removed-- Did we intend for this section header to be in a "full"
13removed-- block?

15removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
16removed-- Is Basics needed explicitly? And why are these here
17removed-- instead of at the top of the file?
18removed
19removed-- Until now, we have been working with our own custom natural
20removed-- numbers, using the `Nat` type that we defined in
21removed-- `Basics.lean`.
22removed
23removed-- However, Lean has a built-in type of natural numbers, which
24removed-- is more powerful and comes with many useful features. They
25removed-- are very slightly different from our custom `Nat`, but these
26removed-- differences are mostly superficial. The built-in natural
27removed-- numbers are defined in the `Init` module, which is
28removed-- automatically imported by Lean. We will refer to them as
29removed-- `Nat` as well, but they are not the same as the `Nat` we
30removed-- defined in `Basics.lean`.
31removed
32removed-- In Lean, programmers and mathematicians don't re-prove the
33removed-- basic properties of natural numbers from scratch, nor do
34removed-- they tend to write out `rewrite` steps for basic properties
35removed-- of natural numbers by hand.
36removed
37removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
38removed-- Just making a note that we need to explain the
39removed-- `zero.succ.succ` notation someplace well before this
40removed-- file!
41removed--
42removed-- Have we already explained sections, and how they differ
43removed-- from namespaces? Will it be clear to readers why we need
44removed-- one here? Can we choose a better name than
45removed-- `long_example`?
46removed
47removed-- Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
48removed-- We turn off the postfix notation for our new definition
49removed-- of succ in `Basics`, should we also turn it off here for
50removed-- Nats? I really find it to be less readable, but maybe
51removed-- that's just me.
52removed
53removedsection long_example
54removedopen NatPlayground.Nat
55removed
56removed-- Previously, we did computation like this...
57removed
58removedtheorem test_mult1' : (two * two : NatPlayground.Nat) = four := by
59removed rewrite [two_eq_succ_one, one_eq_succ_zero]
60removed rewrite [mul_succ, mul_succ, mul_zero]
61removed rewrite [add_succ, add_succ, add_zero]
62removed rewrite [add_succ, add_succ, add_zero]
63removed rfl
64removedend long_example
65removed
66removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, NOW):
67removed-- The info viewed in the InfoView during this proof is
68removed-- kind of mysterious (to me) here. Have we already given
69removed-- people enough help to understand it here?
70removed
71removed-- This approach is useful in a textbook for understanding the
72removed-- structure of natural numbers and for providing early
73removed-- practice with writing proofs. But it is also tedious in the
74removed-- long term.
75removed
76removed-- Instead of doing this, programmers and mathematicians use
77removed-- the built-in `Nat` and the powerful features of Lean to
78removed-- *automatically* prove properties about natural numbers and
79removed-- to compute with them.
80removed
81removedtheorem test_mult1_nat : (3 * 3 : Nat) = 9 := by
82removed rfl
83removed
84removed-- The annotation `: Nat` tells Lean that we are using its
85removed-- built-in `Nat` type.
86removed
87removed-- In this chapter we will learn how to use the built-in `Nat`
88removed-- and some powerful features for computing with and proving
89removed-- properties about natural numbers. Specifically, we will
90removed-- learn about `dsimp`, `calc`, and `simp` annotations, which
91removed-- enable more powerful and concise proofs.
92removed
93removed-- In fact, from now on, we will use the built-in `Nat` type
94removed-- and its powerful features, writing `Nat.<theorem>` to
95removed-- reference Lean's version of `<theorem>`.
96removed
97removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
98removed-- Why can't we just write <theorem>?
99removed
100removed-- ### `rfl` and computation with `Nat`
101removed
102removed-- With Lean's `Nat`, much of the computation happens
103removed-- automatically, and `rfl` suffices to close any equality of
104removed-- computation on literals.
105removed
106removedtheorem complicated_computation : (2 * 3 + 4 * 5 : Nat) * 6 = 156 := by
107removed rfl
108removed
109removed-- This quickly becomes necessary, as natural numbers quickly
110removed-- get large!
111removed
112removed-- Of course, `rfl` can't close more complicated goals where
113removed-- the values of the terms are unknown.
114removed
115removedtheorem rfl_not_enough (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := by
116removed -- rfl will not work here!
117removed /- First rewrite the goal with `h`; then the two sides are identical. -/
118removed rewrite [h]
119removed rfl
120removed
121removed-- The same proof can be written more compactly with `rw`. In
122removed-- this example, `rw [h]` rewrites with `h` and then closes the
123removed-- resulting reflexive goal.
124removed
125removedtheorem rfl_not_enough' (n m : Nat) (h : n = m) : n = m := by
126removed rw [h]
127removed
128removed-- We will continue to show more powerful tools for
129removed-- manipulating the context and goal of a proof to bring them
130removed-- closer to what can be solved with `rfl`.
131removed
132removed-- ## Using the Standard Library
133removed
134removed-- Use the `exact?` tactic to search for relevant theorems in
135removed-- the standard library.
136removed
137removedexample (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := by
138removed /- this will suggest that we use `exact Nat.add_comm a b` to close this goal -/
139removed exact?
140removed
141removed-- You can also use `rw?` to look for theorems to rewrite by
142removed
143removedexample (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := by
144removed /- this will suggest that we use `rw [Nat.add_comm]` to close this goal -/
145removed rw?
146removed
147removedexample (n m q : Nat) :
148removed (n + m) + q = m + (n + q) := by
149removed -- lots of suggestions to look through here!
150removed rw?
151removed sorry
152removed
153removed-- Prove the following theorems about `Nat`s. You should not
154removed-- need induction for any of these; you can find the theorems
155removed-- you need using `rw?` and `exact?`.
156removed
157removedtheorem mul_three (p : Nat) :
158removed 3 * p = p + p + p := by
159removed sorry
160removed
161removedtheorem mul_three_beq (p : Nat) :
162removed (3 * p == p + p + p) = true := by
163removed sorry
164removed
165removed-- ## Structuring proofs with `calc`
166removed
167removed-- In Lean proofs, long `rw` chains are useful, but they are
168removed-- sometimes hard to read because the intermediate goals are
169removed-- invisible. Furthermore, sometimes we *know* exactly how we
170removed-- want to manipulate the terms of a proof, but don't want to
171removed-- have the tactics like `add_comm` and `add_assoc` "guess"
172removed-- which subterms to rewrite.
173removed
174removed-- The `calc` tactic writes down the intermediate goals of a
175removed-- proof, and allows us to specify exactly which rewrite rules
176removed-- to apply at each step. It is a powerful tool for structuring
177removed-- proofs, and is often more readable than long `rw` chains.
178removed
179removed-- `calc` is designed to mimic the style of proofs in
180removed-- mathematics textbooks, which will often look something like
181removed-- this:
182removed
183removed-- a + (b + c)
184removed-- = (a + b) + c ... [by associativity of addition]
185removed-- = (b + a) + c ... [by commutativity of addition]
186removed-- = b + (a + c) ... [by associativity of addition]
187removed
188removed-- Note how we can see each intermediate step of this proof
189removed-- when we look at it this way. Let's look at how we might
190removed-- prove this theorem (i.e., that `a + (b + c) = b + (a + c)`)
191removed-- in Lean.
192removed
193removed-- First, a proof in the style we already know.
194removed
195removedtheorem add_swap (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
196removed rw [← Nat.add_assoc, Nat.add_comm a b, Nat.add_assoc]
197removed
198removed-- Here we present the same theorem, written with `calc`. Note
199removed-- how each intermediate goal is visible in the source.
200removed
201removedtheorem add_swap' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
202removed calc a + (b + c) /- one side of the goal is the argument to `calc`... -/
203removed /- ... and each subsequent line is a transformation, with a tactic. -/
204removed a + (b + c) = (a + b) + c := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
205removed (a + b) + c = (b + a) + c := by rw [Nat.add_comm a b]
206removed /- once a line matches the other side of the equality in the main goal
207removed (in this case `(b + (a + c)`), the calc tactic succeeds. -/
208removed (b + a) + c = b + (a + c) := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
209removed
210removed-- We can also write the proof like this to be a bit more
211removed-- concise:
212removed
213removedtheorem add_swap'' (a b c : Nat) : a + (b + c) = b + (a + c) := by
214removed calc a + (b + c)
215removed _ = (a + b) + c := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
216removed _ = (b + a) + c := by rw [Nat.add_comm a b]
217removed _ = b + (a + c) := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
218removed
219removed-- Whereas before, the left-hand side of each equality in the
220removed-- `calc` tactic was repeated from the right-hand side of the
221removed-- previous one, we can replace the left-hand side entirely
222removed-- with an `_`. Now our Lean proof looks quite a bit like the
223removed-- textbook one we saw earlier!
224removed
225removed-- ### Exercise (1 star): succ_mul_succ ⭐
226removed
227removedtheorem succ_mul_succ (n m : Nat) :
228removed (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := by
229removed rw [Nat.add_mul, Nat.one_mul, Nat.mul_add, Nat.mul_one, ← Nat.add_assoc]
230removed
231removed-- Given this proof with `rw`, rewrite it with `calc`. Reminder
232removed-- that you can use `rw?` to find appropriate rules to rewrite
233removed-- by.
234removed
235removedtheorem succ_mul_succ' (n m : Nat) :
236removed (n + 1) * (m + 1) = n * m + n + m + 1 := by
237removed sorry
238removed
239removed-- If you prefer `rw` to `calc`, that's fine! Each has
240removed-- particular uses, and both will be tools in your ever-growing
241removed-- toolbox of tactics.
242removed
243removed-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
244removed-- Needs some exercises!!
245removed
246removed-- ## Definitional simplification: `dsimp`
247removed
248removed-- Often, rather than rewriting by a known equation like
249removed
250removed-- `n + succ m = succ (n + m)` using `rw [add_succ]`,
251removed
252removed-- we just want to simplify the function (here `add`)
253removed-- automatically when we can.
254removed
255removed-- The `dsimp` tactic ("definitionally simplify") unfolds
256removed-- definitions and performs definitional simplifications. You
257removed-- can give it hints in square brackets: `dsimp [f]` tells it
258removed-- to unfold the definition of `f`. You can also simplify a
259removed-- hypothesis `h` in the context by writing `dsimp [...] at h`.
260removed-- `dsimp` will also close goals by `rfl` when possible.
261removed
262removeddef square (n : Nat) : Nat := n * n
263removed
264removeddef triple (n : Nat) : Nat := n + n + n
265removed
266removed-- When the goal depends on a fact about an unknown value,
267removed-- `rfl` fails. Here, `dsimp` makes progress, exposing a goal
268removed-- the fact can close.
269removed
270removedexample (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := by
271removed -- rfl will not work here!
272removed dsimp [triple]
273removed /- The goal can now be rewritten by `h`. -/
274removed rw [h]
275removed
276removed-- As we have seen, `rw` can also unfold definitions. In this
277removed-- example, either style is fine: use `dsimp [triple]` when you
278removed-- want to emphasize definitional simplification, or
279removed-- `rw [triple, h]` when the proof is just a sequence of
280removed-- rewrites.
281removed
282removedexample (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := by
283removed /- `rw [triple]` unfolds `triple n`. -/
284removed rw [triple, h]
285removed
286removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): dsimp1 ⭐⭐
287removed
288removed-- Complete this proof, using `dsimp` or `rw` as appropriate.
289removed
290removedexample (n m : Nat) (h : m = n) : triple m = n + (n + n) := by
291removed sorry
292removed
293removed-- `dsimp at h` also works on hypotheses, which rfl can't
294removed-- touch.
295removed
296removedexample (n : Nat) (h : square n = 16) : n * n = 16 := by
297removed dsimp [square] at h
298removed exact h
299removed
300removed-- Aside: `rw [...] at h` also works on hypotheses too, as does
301removed-- `rw? at h`
302removed
303removedexample (n m : Nat) (h : 2 * n = m * 2) : n + n = m + m := by
304removed rw [Nat.mul_comm, Nat.mul_two, Nat.mul_two] at h
305removed exact h
306removed
307removed-- `dsimp` also takes definitional steps such as `+ 0`, so it
308removed-- can finish goals that rfl would close.
309removed
310removedexample (n : Nat) : square n + 0 = n * n := by
311removed dsimp [square]
312removed

314removed-- searches for functions to simplify by. Many Lean tactics
315removed-- have `?` versions; try it out if you are unsure.

326removed-- ## Redefining Functions and Lemmas over Nats
327removed
328removed-- Let's redefine some functions on Lean's `Nat`s and prove
329removed-- some theorems about them.
330removed
331removeddef Nat.even (n : Nat) :=
332removed match n with
333removed | 0 => true
334removed | 1 => false
335removed | n + 2 => even n
336removed
337removeddef Nat.odd (n : Nat) := !(even n)
338removed
339removedtheorem Nat.odd_def (n : Nat) : n.odd = !(n.even) := rfl
340removed
341removeddef Nat.minustwo (n : Nat) : Nat :=
342removed match n with
343removed | 0 => 0
344removed | 1 => 0
345removed | n' + 2 => n'
346removed
347removeddef Nat.double (n : Nat) : Nat :=
348removed match n with
349removed | 0 => 0
350removed | n' + 1 => double n' + 2
351removed
352removed-- Defining functions in the `Nat` namespace changes how they
353removed-- print:
354removed
355removedtheorem even_add_three (n : Nat) : Nat.even (n + 3) = Nat.even (n + 1) := by
356removed rfl
357removed
358removed-- This printing style is called *field notation* and can be
359removed-- disabled with the `pp_nodot` attribute.
360removed
361removedexample (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := by
362removed rfl
363removed
364removedattribute [pp_nodot] Nat.double
365removed
366removedexample (n : Nat) : Nat.double (n + 0) = Nat.double n := by
367removed rfl
368removed
369removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): even_succ ⭐⭐
370removed
371removedtheorem even_succ (n : Nat) :
372removed (n + 1).even = !(n.even) := by
373removed sorry
374removed
375removed-- Note to developers (NOW):
376removed-- talk about using `Nat.add_zero` and friends from now on.
377removed
378removed-- (OA) : added lemmas proved for our Nat for Lean's Nat to
379removed-- prevent later files from breaking.
380removed
381removedtheorem even_zero : Nat.even 0 = true := by rfl
382removed
383removedtheorem double_zero : Nat.double 0 = 0 := by rfl
384removed
385removedtheorem double_succ (n : Nat) : (n + 1).double = n.double + 2 := by rfl
386removed
387removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): double_add ⭐⭐
388removed
389removedtheorem double_add (n : Nat) : n.double = n + n := by
390removed sorry
391removed
392removed-- ### Exercise (2 stars): double_mul ⭐⭐
393removed
394removedtheorem double_mul (n : Nat) : n.double = 2 * n := by
395removed sorry

397removed-- ## Using Code Actions to Generate Match Skeletons
398removed
399removed-- Lean's language server can suggest *code actions*, which are
400removed-- small editor commands that modify the source code. In
401removed-- VSCode, a light-bulb icon appears on the left when a code
402removed-- action is available at your cursor. You can click the icon
403removed-- or open the code action menu with `Ctrl + .` on
404removed-- Windows/Linux or `Command + .` on macOS.
405removed
406removed-- For more information, see [Lean 4 VS Code extension
407removed-- manual](https://github.com/leanprover/vscode-lean4/blob/master/vscode-lean4/manual/manual.md#code-actions).
408removed
409removed-- Some code actions can generate the explicit branches needed
410removed-- for pattern matching. This is especially useful when working
411removed-- with `match` expressions, or with tactics such as `cases`
412removed-- and `induction`, which we saw in previous chapters.
413removed
414removed-- Let's look at an example using `induction`.
